speaker: Karina Nguyen
title: The Agent Reasoning Interface: Claude, ChatGPT Canvas, Tasks, Operator — with Karina Nguyen
question: In frontier LLM benchmarking, why hasn't the industry converged on a single standardized evaluation harness that every lab runs?
guest: I think it operates on an assumption that the next generation of the model or the model you produce next is going to behave the same. For example, the way you prompt o1 or Claude 3 is going to be very different from each other. There is a lot of prompting that you need to do to get the evals to run correctly. Sometimes the model will just output extra new lines, and the way it gets parsed will be incorrect. This happened with Stanford's HELM benchmarks—Claude was always not performing well, and that was because the way they prompted it was kind of wrong. Even with structured output, each eval can work in a very different way. Sometimes you ask the model to output in XML tags, but some models are not really good at XML tags. So do you change the formatting per model, or do you run the same format across all models? And then there are the metrics themselves—maybe accuracy is one thing, but maybe you care about some other metrics like F-score. It's just very hard.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
There is no single harness because the incentives, the technology, and the science all pull against one.

Results depend heavily on scaffolding: prompt format, system prompts, tool access, reasoning budget, retry policy, sampling settings and answer-grading rules. Each lab's models are tuned for different setups, so any "neutral" harness would favour some models and handicap others. Labs also want to show their best-case capability, which means a custom scaffold, while others report minimal-elicitation numbers; both are defensible but not comparable.

The target also keeps moving. Benchmarks saturate or get contaminated by training data within a year or two, and agentic evaluations (coding, computer use, long-horizon tasks) need complex environments where the harness is effectively part of the system being tested. A standard frozen today would be obsolete quickly.

Finally, there is no neutral body with the authority, funding and access to enforce one. Model APIs differ in features, some evaluations are kept private to prevent gaming, and benchmark scores are marketing assets.

Partial convergence does exist, through shared frameworks like Inspect and third-party evaluators such as METR, Artificial Analysis and the government AI safety institutes.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer: Frontier LLM benchmarking resists a single standardized harness because evaluation is inseparable from rapidly evolving model interfaces, infrastructure, and incentives. Early harnesses assumed raw log-probabilities and static few-shot prompts, whereas modern frontier models rely on proprietary chat templates, reasoning traces, tool-use loops, and API-only endpoints. Because small differences in prompt formatting, answer extraction, or sampling parameters can swing scores substantially, any rigid harness inadvertently favors models post-trained on matching conventions while penalizing others. Labs also disagree on methodology—specifically whether evaluations should enforce identical prompts or measure peak capability under model-specific scaffolding. Meanwhile, rapid benchmark saturation and contamination continually push frontier testing away from static text tasks toward stateful, sandboxed environments, such as containerized software engineering and computer-use agents, which must integrate tightly with each lab's internal cluster orchestration and security infrastructure. Finally, competitive incentives discourage convergence: labs naturally prefer configurations that highlight their models' strengths and avoid coupling unreleased checkpoints or confidential inference stacks to external codebases they do not control.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer: The main reason is that results depend heavily on harness choices that are hard to agree on, and labs have reasons not to give those choices up. Scores can move several points with prompt format, few-shot examples, chat templates, sampling temperature, answer-extraction rules, tool access and scaffolding. That matters most for agentic tasks like SWE-bench, where the scaffold is effectively part of the system being tested. Each lab tunes these settings to show its model well and to match how the model is actually used, so a single fixed setup feels unfair to someone. Capabilities also change faster than any standard can keep up: benchmarks saturate or leak into training data within months, so whatever a consortium standardized would soon be stale. Some evaluations can't be shared at all, such as private held-out sets, safety and dangerous-capability tests, and internal agent environments. Finally, no neutral body has the authority or compute budget to impose one. What exists instead is a patchwork of shared tools (EleutherAI's lm-evaluation-harness, HELM, Inspect, OpenAI's simple-evals) plus independent third-party evaluators like Epoch AI, Artificial Analysis and LMArena. Lab-reported numbers still aren't fully comparable with each other.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer: The industry has not converged on a single evaluation harness because technical, methodological, and competitive forces all pull against standardization. Technically, frontier models are highly sensitive to prompt formatting, system instructions, reasoning budgets, and agentic scaffolding; a fixed harness that works cleanly for one model's tool-use or thinking style can artificially depress another's performance. Methodologically, frontier capabilities evolve faster than consensus standards can form, particularly for long-horizon coding, multimodal, and agentic tasks where grading requires complex environments or imperfect LLM judges. Furthermore, any single canonical harness quickly becomes a target for Goodhart's Law, inviting accidental contamination or subtle optimization to the harness's quirks rather than genuine capability. Finally, labs face misaligned incentives: each has invested heavily in internal evaluation pipelines tied to its own serving infrastructure, and none wants to cede control over how its flagship releases are framed to a third-party harness that might disadvantage its architecture or product priorities. As a result, labs rely on internal harnesses for iteration while third-party evaluators provide independent—though still varied—cross-lab comparisons.
